description: Knowledge base v1 (D7): short passages in our own words. scheme_rule passages paraphrase a public source; team_runbook passages are our own operational guidance and must be labelled as team guidance, never as a scheme rule.

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AC01 (incorrect account number): the beneficiary's bank could not use the IBAN, either because its format is invalid or because the IBAN does not exist at that bank. The EPC lists the likely root causes as the beneficiary giving an invalid IBAN, the originator using wrong IBAN data from its own customer records, or a technical problem when the originator created the instruction. Suggested next step: the originator contacts the beneficiary to obtain the beneficiary's correct IBAN.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AC01

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AC04 (closed account number): the beneficiary's account is closed at the beneficiary's bank, typically because the beneficiary closed it after the originator last paid them. Suggested next step per the EPC: the originator contacts the beneficiary to obtain their new account. Some SEPA countries do not allow AC04 for data-protection reasons; banks there may send MS03 instead, so the same situation can arrive under a different code. AC04 is also used as a negative answer to a recall or a request for recall.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AC04

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AC06 (blocked account): the beneficiary's bank has blocked the account for any financial transaction. The EPC describes two kinds of cases: a block because of a court order, or a block the bank placed itself, for example on suspicion of misuse or at the beneficiary's own request. Suggested next step: the originator contacts the beneficiary to agree an alternative account or another way to pay.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AC06

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AG01 (transaction forbidden): SCT Inst payments cannot be booked on this type of account, usually because the beneficiary gave the details of such an account. Suggested next steps per the EPC: the originator contacts the beneficiary to agree on another payment instrument. In addition, subject to applicable law, the originator's bank may re-initiate the payment as a standard (non-instant) SEPA credit transfer, but only if the originator and its bank agreed this beforehand.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AG01

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AM05 (duplication): the clearing system or the beneficiary's bank considered that an identical SCT Inst payment had been sent or processed very recently, and stopped this one as a duplicate. The EPC names a technical or human error at the originator or at the originator's bank as the root cause. Suggested next step: the originator and its bank check whether the payment really was duplicated.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AM05

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with AB05 (timeout at the creditor agent): the beneficiary's bank did not receive the payment within the time-out deadline set by the SCT Inst rulebook, or within a shorter deadline agreed between banks. The EPC says the cause can be a connection, processing or validation problem anywhere from the originator's bank, through the clearing system or systems, to the beneficiary's bank. Suggested next steps: the originator's bank suggests that the originator re-issue the instant payment later or use another instrument such as a standard SEPA credit transfer; the originator may also contact the beneficiary for another way to pay.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code AB05

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with MS02 (reason not specified, customer generated): the beneficiary refused the payment when it was presented. The beneficiary's bank is acting on the beneficiary's own instruction not to accept funds from a particular account, from a particular originator, or through a particular payment scheme. No further reason is given. Suggested next step per the EPC: the originator contacts the beneficiary directly to agree how to settle whatever the originator owes the beneficiary.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code MS02

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with MS03 (reason not specified, agent generated): the beneficiary's bank rejected the payment without a specific reason. The EPC allows MS03 only where national law, such as data-protection law, forbids the more precise codes AC04, RR01, RR02, RR03 or RR04, and asks banks to limit its use. The underlying cause may therefore be a closed account or a regulatory reason. Suggested next step: the originator contacts the beneficiary directly to agree how to settle the obligation.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code MS03

passages.text: SEPA Instant reject with RR04 (regulatory reason): the beneficiary's bank stopped the payment for a regulatory reason other than those covered by RR01, RR02 or RR03. The EPC gives a potential hit for anti-money-laundering, embargo or counter-terrorist-financing reasons as the root cause. Some SEPA countries forbid RR04 for data-protection reasons, and banks there may use MS03 instead. Suggested next step per the EPC: the originator contacts its own bank, the originator PSP.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, code RR04

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with AC01 (incorrect account number): the debtor's IBAN has an invalid format or does not exist at the debtor's bank; a return is only used for the second case. The EPC lists the root causes as the debtor giving wrong data, the creditor using wrong IBAN data from its customer records, or a technical problem when the creditor created the collection. Suggested creditor actions: contact the debtor to get the correct IBAN, and if the mandate was amended, check the data the debtor provided.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AC01

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with AC04 (closed account number): the debtor's account is closed at the debtor's bank, typically because the debtor closed it after the creditor's last collection from that account. Suggested creditor action per the EPC: contact the debtor for the new account. In some SEPA countries data-protection rules forbid AC04, and banks there may send MS03 instead, so the same situation can arrive under that code.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AC04

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with AC06 (blocked account): the debtor's account, or this particular collection, is blocked. The EPC describes two kinds of cases: a block because of a court order, or a block placed by the debtor's bank itself, for example on suspicion of misuse or at the debtor's request. Suggested creditor action: contact the debtor to agree an alternative account or another way to pay. The guidance notes that the creditor's bank can take such actions on the creditor's behalf where this has been agreed.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AC06 and footnote 1

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with AG01 (transaction forbidden): direct debits cannot be booked from this type of account for regulatory reasons, a savings account being the EPC's example, because the debtor gave the details of such an account. The EPC adds that AG01 must not be used when an SDD B2B collection is presented to a consumer account; code AC13 applies in that case. Suggested creditor action: contact the debtor to agree on another payment account or another payment instrument.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AG01

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with AM04 (insufficient funds): the debtor's account did not hold enough money to cover the full amount of the collection. Besides the debtor's balance, the EPC names a creditor-side root cause: missing or late pre-notification announcing the collection date and amount. Suggested creditor action: contact the debtor so that the debtor makes funds available on the account. Some SEPA countries forbid AM04 for data-protection reasons, and banks there may send MS03 instead.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AM04

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject, return or reversal with AM05 (duplication): the clearing system or the debtor's bank considered that an identical collection had been sent or processed very recently, and treated this one as a duplicate. The EPC names a technical or human error at the creditor or at the creditor's bank as the root cause. Suggested creditor action: check whether the collection really was duplicated.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code AM05

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject, return or refund with MD01 (no mandate): the debtor's bank found no valid mandate for the collection, or the debtor claimed a refund of an unauthorised collection. Among the root causes, the EPC lists a creditor that did not use a unique mandate reference, or used one that does not match the mandate information, and a debtor who cancelled the mandate. Suggested creditor actions: analyse the characteristics of the collection, and in the case of a refund, contact the debtor.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code MD01

passages.text: MD01 (no mandate) covers several different SEPA Direct Debit situations, which the EPC lists exhaustively: no mandate exists; a B2B mandate has not yet been confirmed by the debtor; the debtor's bank could not obtain the B2B mandate; the debtor's bank cancelled the mandate under the rule on 36 months without collections; or, for SDD Core only, the debtor requested a refund of an unauthorised transaction, which is possible until 13 months after the debit date. The reason code alone does not say which situation applies.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code MD01 (exhaustive list of use-cases)

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit refund with MD06 (refund request by end customer): the debtor used the unconditional right to a refund of an authorised SDD Core collection, which applies until 8 weeks after the debit date. The EPC links this to the refund right under the Payment Services Directive, and mentions a mismatch between the pre-notified amount and the amount actually collected as one possible trigger. MD06 applies to SDD Core collections only. Suggested creditor action: contact the debtor.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code MD06

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject, return, reversal or refusal with MS02 (reason not specified, customer generated): the debtor refused the collection when it was presented, for example after receiving the pre-notification and deciding not to pay. The decision came from the debtor, not from the debtor's bank, and no further reason is given. Suggested creditor action per the EPC: contact the debtor.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code MS02

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject, return or reversal with MS03 (reason not specified, agent generated): the debtor's bank gave no specific reason. The EPC allows MS03 only where national law, such as data-protection law, forbids the precise codes AC04, AM04, MD07, RR01, RR02, RR03 and RR04, and asks banks to limit its use. The underlying cause may therefore be a closed account, insufficient funds, a deceased debtor or a regulatory reason. Suggested creditor action: contact the debtor.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code MS03

passages.text: SEPA Direct Debit reject or return with RR04 (regulatory reason): the debtor's bank stopped the collection for a regulatory reason other than those covered by RR01, RR02 or RR03. Some SEPA countries forbid RR04 for data-protection reasons, and banks there may use MS03 instead. Suggested creditor action per the EPC: contact the creditor's own bank, the creditor PSP. Unlike most SDD reason codes, the guidance does not suggest contacting the debtor here.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, code RR04

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with AC03 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the creditor account number is invalid or missing. Our first-line team handles it. Ask the customer to confirm the recipient's account number directly with the recipient before sending a new payment, and do not resubmit with the same details. If several AC03 rejections hit the same saved payee, check whether the customer's saved payee details are wrong.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of AC03; route from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with AC04 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the account number specified has been closed on the books of the bank holding the account. Our first-line team handles it. Tell the customer that the recipient's account is closed and ask them to get current account details from the recipient. Do not retry the payment to the same account, and do not suggest that the recipient's bank made an error.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of AC04; route from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with AC06 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the account specified is blocked, prohibiting posting of transactions against it. Our first-line team handles it. Tell the customer that the recipient's account cannot accept the payment and suggest they agree another account or payment method with the recipient. Do not guess or share why the account is blocked; that decision belongs to the recipient's bank.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of AC06; route from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with AG01 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the transaction is forbidden on this type of account. Our routing table sends RTP AG01 to the developer team rather than first line. The developer team first checks whether anything on our side, such as configuration or message content, caused the rejection. If nothing is wrong on our side, first line asks the customer to agree another payment method with the recipient.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of AG01; route_by_rail from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with AM04 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the funds available are insufficient to cover the message amount. Our routing table sends RTP AM04 to Treasury, not to first line. Treasury checks our bank's own funding position for RTP before anyone contacts the customer. Do not tell the customer they lack funds unless Treasury confirms that the cause was on the customer's side; until then the customer message stays neutral.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of AM04; route_by_rail from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: Team guidance, not a scheme rule: an RTP rejection with DS24 means, per the ISO 20022 definition, that the waiting time expired due to an incomplete order, so the payment timed out and was not completed. Our routing table sends it to the developer team, who check our connection and processing logs for this payment. Before anyone resends, confirm the original payment's final status (pacs.028 status request) to avoid a duplicate payment. First line may suggest that the customer try again later or use another payment method, without promising when it will work.
passages.source_section: Team runbook; ISO 20022 ExternalStatusReason1Code definition of DS24; route from reason_codes.json
passages.review_note: Team runbook signed off by Akshay; built from the ISO definition and our routing table.

passages.text: In SEPA Instant, FRAD (fraudulent origin) is a recall reason, not a reject reason. The originator or its bank uses it after detecting a fraudulent SCT Inst payment, either because the originator says it was the victim of a fraudulently executed payment, or because fraudsters manipulated the bank's SCT Inst systems. A recall is a separate message from the status reports and returns this explainer reads. If the beneficiary side accepts the recall, the funds come back with reason FOCR, so the fraud reason does not appear on that return.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, codes FRAD and FOCR

passages.text: In SEPA Instant, exception handling uses three kinds of R-transaction: rejects, recalls, and requests for recall by the originator (RFRO). Which one applies depends on when the problem is detected and who acts. Rejects carry codes such as AC01, AC04 or AB05. The originator or its bank starts a recall for duplicate sending (DUPL), a technical problem (TECH) or fraudulent origin (FRAD). An RFRO is the originator's own request to recover settled funds, for example after paying a wrong IBAN or a higher amount than intended. All R-transactions go through the same clearing system as the original payment unless the banks agree otherwise.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 1; section 3, codes DUPL, TECH, FRAD, AC03, AM09

passages.text: SEPA Instant recall window: only the originator's bank can start a recall, possibly on the originator's behalf, and only for duplicate sending, technical problems that produced an erroneous payment, or a fraudulently originated instruction (FRAD). The recall must be sent within 10 banking business days of the original payment's execution date for duplicates and technical problems, and within 13 months for fraud. Only one recall can be sent per payment. The originator's bank may refuse a customer's recall request that falls outside these reasons or time limits.
passages.source_section: EPC004-16 2025 SCT Inst Rulebook v1.1, section 4.3.2.2 'SCT Inst Recall' (page 39) and rule CT-02.01R
passages.review_note: Both figures verified against the 2025 SCT Inst Rulebook v1.1 on 2026-10-15.

passages.text: Answer deadline for SEPA Instant recalls: the beneficiary's bank is in breach of the SCT Inst rulebook if it does not answer a recall, or a request for recall by the originator, within 15 banking business days of receiving it from the originator's bank. A positive answer returns the funds with reason code FOCR (following cancellation request). A negative answer can carry codes such as CUST (the beneficiary refuses), AC04 (account closed) or AM04 (not enough funds left on the beneficiary's account to debit the amount).
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 1; section 3, codes FOCR, CUST, AC04, AM04

passages.text: What a SEPA Instant recall can and cannot achieve: a recall or a request for recall is only a request. The beneficiary can refuse it (reason CUST), for example by claiming to be entitled to the funds, and the beneficiary's account may lack the funds or be closed. After a negative answer, the EPC's suggested action is for the originator to contact the beneficiary directly to recover the money outside the recall procedure. It follows that a customer message must not promise that money will come back, or when.
passages.source_section: EPC059-18 v7.0, section 3, codes CUST, AM04, AC04

passages.text: In SEPA Direct Debit, exception handling uses five kinds of R-transaction: refusals, rejects, returns, refunds and reversals. Which one applies depends on when in the processing chain the problem is detected and who starts it; the SDD Core and SDD B2B rulebooks define them in their section 4.4. Rejects, returns and refunds must go through the same clearing system as the original collection unless the banks agree otherwise. The same reason code can arrive as different types: AM05, for example, can be a reject, a return or a reversal.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 1; section 3, code AM05

passages.text: SDD Core refund rights, as described in the EPC's reason-code guidance: a debtor can obtain an unconditional refund of an authorised SDD Core collection until 8 weeks after the debit date (reason MD06), linked to the refund right in the Payment Services Directive. For an unauthorised SDD Core collection, the debtor can claim a refund until 13 months after the debit date (reason MD01). Both refund types are listed for SDD Core collections only. For a creditor, a refund can therefore arrive weeks or months after a collection appeared successful.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, codes MD06 and MD01

passages.text: SDD B2B differs from SDD Core on refunds: the EPC's guidance lists both the unconditional refund (MD06) and the refund of an unauthorised collection (MD01) for SDD Core collections only. B2B collections have their own mandate checks instead. A B2B collection can be rejected or returned with MD01 when the debtor has not confirmed the B2B mandate to its bank, or when the debtor's bank could not obtain it. A B2B collection presented to a consumer account must be rejected with AC13 rather than AG01.
passages.source_section: EPC173-14 v8.0, section 3, codes MD06, MD01 and AG01

passages.text: The RTP network is strictly credit push: the payer's bank sends the money. According to The Clearing House, a sending bank cannot revoke or recall a payment once it has been submitted to the network, and settlement is final and irrevocable. TCH presents this irrevocability as protecting payees from returns or reversals. Instead of a recall, the network provides a message that lets a bank request the return of funds. The network operates 24/7, so payments can be sent or received at any time.
passages.source_section: TCH public RTP page for financial institutions (FAQ)

passages.text: RTP Request for Return of Funds, as described by The Clearing House: the sending bank may send this request to the receiving bank for any reason, for example a payment sent to the wrong person. It is only a request: the receiving bank is under no obligation to return the funds. Its response is either negative or positive, and if it agrees, it returns the money by sending a new payment that credits the original sender. Once the receiving bank has responded, the sender cannot submit another request for the same payment.
passages.source_section: TCH Payments Pulse, 1 Nov 2023, 'We Get Questions', Instant Payments (citing RTP Operating Rules section VII.D)
passages.caveat: Published TCH newsletter from November 2023; the current Operating Rules may have changed since.

passages.text: Response time for an RTP Request for Return of Funds, per The Clearing House's published Q&A on its Operating Rules: the receiving bank must respond within 10 banking days. Claims of fraud or of breach of warranty are exceptions, where the receiving bank may take longer to complete its investigation. The deadline is for a response, not for a refund, because the response can be negative. The source is a TCH newsletter from November 2023, so the current Operating Rules may differ.
passages.source_section: TCH Payments Pulse, 1 Nov 2023, 'We Get Questions', Instant Payments (citing RTP Operating Rules section VII.D)
passages.caveat: Published TCH newsletter from November 2023; the current Operating Rules may have changed since.

passages.text: No tipping off: under Article 39 of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive, Directive (EU) 2015/849, a bank, its directors and its employees must not tell the customer concerned, or any other third party, that information has been, is being or will be reported under the Directive's reporting duties, or that a money-laundering or terrorist-financing analysis is under way or may take place. Disclosure to competent authorities, or for law-enforcement purposes, is allowed. For regulatory stops such as RR04, customer messages therefore stay neutral and give no reason.
passages.source_section: Directive (EU) 2015/849, Article 39(1)-(2), adopted text (official version: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2015/849/oj)
passages.caveat: Checked against the adopted text as republished on legislation.gov.uk. Later amendments added group-sharing exceptions; paragraphs 1-2 as summarised here are unchanged in substance.

passages.text: The EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), applies from 10 July 2027, and from 10 July 2029 for football agents and certain professional football club transactions. The Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (MLD4, Directive 2015/849) is repealed with effect from 10 July 2027. The tipping-off rule cited in KB-ALL-GEN-01 comes from that Directive, so from July 2027 staff should check the AMLR's own disclosure rules before relying on that passage.
passages.source_section: A&O Shearman FinReg, 'Package of EU Anti-Money Laundering Legislation Published' (19 June 2024); official text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1624/oj
passages.review_note: Dates verified against the A&O Shearman summary on 2026-10-15; AMLR article number deliberately not cited.
